article.title: GitHub Restructures Bug Bounty Program, Cutting Public Payouts in Half and Reserving Top Rewards for a New VIP Tier
article.summary: Effective July 27, GitHub is cutting public bug bounty payouts and creating an invite-only VIP tier, following curl's earlier bounty collapse under AI-generated reports.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

GitHub is overhauling its bug bounty program, cutting public payouts by at least half at every severity level while creating a permanent, invite-only tier that pays significantly more, according to a [GitHub Blog post](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/) published July 22. The changes take effect July 27, and the company says they are meant to address what it calls "an increasing queue" of submissions, [GitHub wrote](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/).

The restructuring makes GitHub the latest and largest platform to rework the economics of its bug bounty program in response to a wave of AI-assisted vulnerability reports — a trend that pushed curl, the widely used data-transfer library, to eliminate its own cash bounty entirely earlier this year, [as previously reported](/article/2026-02/22-ai-generated-slop-is-overwhelming-open-source-projects-forcing-emergency-countermeasures).

## What's Changing

Under GitHub's new public bounty table, payouts drop to fixed amounts of $250 for low-severity findings, $2,000 for medium, $5,000 for high, and $10,000 for critical vulnerabilities, [GitHub said](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). According to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html), those figures replace prior ranges of $617-$2,000 for low, $4,000-$10,000 for medium, $10,000-$20,000 for high, and $20,000-$30,000+ for critical reports — a reduction the outlet calculated at roughly 50 percent for medium, high, and critical findings and about 59 percent for low-severity reports, measured against the bottom of the old ranges.

GitHub framed the shift from ranges to flat numbers as a matter of clarity rather than just cost-cutting. "Ranges sound flexible, but in practice they create uncertainty for researchers and overhead for our team," the company wrote, adding that static payouts "set clear expectations on both sides" while leaving room for discretionary bonuses on exceptional work, [per the GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/).

Alongside the public-program cuts, GitHub is formalizing what it calls a "permanent private/invite-only VIP program for qualified researchers who consistently deliver high-quality, high-impact work," [GitHub said](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). VIP payouts are set at $1,000 for low-severity findings, $7,500 for medium, $20,000 for high, and $30,000 or more for critical vulnerabilities — matching or exceeding the top of the old public ranges. To qualify, a researcher must have delivered at least one critical finding, two high findings, four medium findings, or seven low findings, according to the company's published criteria. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) noted that GitHub's announcement does not specify a time window for meeting those thresholds or say whether qualifying guarantees an invitation, and that the company has not disclosed the HackerOne "Signal" score threshold it will enforce on the public program — only that researchers below it will be capped at four initial submissions.

GitHub summarized the incentive change in blunt terms: "You don't earn more by submitting more," the company wrote. "You earn more by submitting better," [according to the GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). Reports filed before July 27 — including those already sitting in GitHub's queue — will still be paid under the old structure, [the company said](https://github.blog/security/next-chapter-restructuring-githubs-bug-bounty-program/).

## The May Preview

July's payout cuts follow a [May 15 GitHub Blog post](https://github.blog/security/raising-the-bar-quality-shared-responsibility-and-the-future-of-githubs-bug-bounty-program/) that first raised the bar on what counts as an acceptable submission, requiring a working proof of concept with demonstrated security impact and explicit validation of any AI-assisted output before it reaches GitHub's triage queue. That post attributed the tightening to an industry-wide surge: "submission volume across the industry has grown significantly. New tools, including AI, have lowered the barrier to entry for security research," GitHub wrote, while cautioning that alongside legitimate reports it had seen "a sharp increase in submissions that don't demonstrate real security impact," [per the company](https://github.blog/security/raising-the-bar-quality-shared-responsibility-and-the-future-of-githubs-bug-bounty-program/). GitHub also began rewarding low-risk, non-exploitable findings with company swag instead of a cash bounty as part of that May update.

The company has repeated the same framing on AI tooling across both posts. "The tools don't matter," GitHub wrote in May. "The quality of the work does," [the company said](https://github.blog/security/raising-the-bar-quality-shared-responsibility-and-the-future-of-githubs-bug-bounty-program/) — language [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) quoted again in its coverage of the July changes.

## The curl Precedent

GitHub's move echoes, in less drastic form, a path curl took months earlier. Lead maintainer Daniel Stenberg ended curl's bug bounty program outright on January 31, 2026, after its confirmed-vulnerability rate "plummeted to below 5%" from a historical rate of "somewhere north of 15%," [Stenberg wrote on his blog](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/01/26/the-end-of-the-curl-bug-bounty/). Stenberg described an "explosion in AI slop reports" that made the program unsustainable and cut off monetary rewards entirely rather than adjust the pay scale.

By contrast to GitHub's approach of tightening reward structure while keeping the program open, curl's initial response was a full stop — but it did not last. In a [follow-up post in April](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/04/22/high-quality-chaos/), Stenberg wrote that curl returned to HackerOne in March 2026 "once we had figured out that GitHub was not good enough" as a private-reporting channel. By April, he reported, submission volume was "about double the rate we had through 2025," but the confirmed-vulnerability rate had recovered to "somewhere in the 15-16% range" — back above curl's pre-AI historical baseline. "Almost every security report now uses AI to various degrees," Stenberg wrote. Unlike the earlier slop wave, he added: "The slop situation is not a problem anymore."

That trajectory — an initial flood of low-effort AI-generated reports followed by a recovery in quality as tooling matured and reporting norms adjusted — is the same dynamic GitHub's two-stage response (the May quality bar, then the July payout restructuring) appears designed to manage without abandoning its public program altogether.

## Analysis

GitHub's framing treats the July changes as a continuation of the May policy, not a separate reaction. Both posts single out volume and validation as the core problem, and both insist that AI-assisted research itself is welcome as long as a human researcher verifies the output before submitting. [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/github-cuts-public-bug-bounty-payouts.html) situated the announcement within a broader pattern in which AI tools simultaneously make it cheaper to generate plausible-looking findings and cheaper for internal security teams to triage and patch code before an external report ever arrives — pointing to Google's newly introduced Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber model, positioned for repeated automated repository scanning, as one example of the latter trend.

What is harder to assess from the public record is whether GitHub's specific thresholds — a fixed $10,000 top public payout, a VIP bar set at one critical or two high findings — will reproduce curl's recovery or instead push away researchers who have not yet built a HackerOne track record. GitHub has not disclosed the Signal score itself, only that newcomers get four submissions before it applies.

## What We Don't Know

GitHub has not published the HackerOne Signal threshold its public program will enforce, nor a timeline for when VIP invitations will go out to researchers who meet the qualification criteria. It is also not yet clear how many researchers currently in GitHub's triage backlog will be grandfathered under the old payout structure before the July 27 cutoff, or how the company will measure whether the restructuring achieves its stated goal of reducing queue volume without discouraging legitimate first-time reporters.
